readerTitle: Your first hire: extra hands or an owner?
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (금속 브래킷 공방, 물리치료 클리닉용 예약 소프트웨어) + 가상 적용 (애견 미용실 예약 앱) + 실제 연구 (Stanford Project on Emerging Companies). 모든 수치는 설명용이며, 연구 결과는 일반적인 수준으로만 서술했습니다.
insight: 첫 채용은 일손을 늘리는 것이 아니라, 창업자를 거쳐야만 돌아가던 결과 하나를 통째로 넘기는 일이다.
misconception: 첫 직원은 시키는 일을 잘 해내는 성실한 조수나, 미래 조직도에 맞춘 전문가면 된다.

sources.text: Baron, J. N., & Hannan, M. T. (2002). Organizational Blueprints for Success in High-Tech Start-Ups: Lessons from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies. California Management Review, 44(3).
공방, 소프트웨어 회사, 애견 미용 앱 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 3번 카드 차트의 주당 근무 시간(70→64, 70→52)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 데이터처럼 보이지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 라벨을 붙였습니다.

Stanford Project on Emerging Companies(SPEC): 1990년대 실리콘밸리 기술 스타트업 약 200곳을 추적한 연구입니다. 창업자의 초기 고용 모델(blueprint)이 성장 후에도 유지되는 경향이 있었고, 나중에 모델을 바꾼 기업은 직원 이직 증가 등 혼란을 겪었다는 내용입니다. 게시 전에 Baron & Hannan(2002) 원문에서 '약 200곳'과 이직 관련 서술을 다시 확인하세요.
8번 카드 앱 사례(유료 미용실 300곳, 주 15시간 지원 업무)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
7번 카드의 '유급 시범 프로젝트' 제안은 일반적인 조언입니다. 특정 국가의 고용법이나 계약 형태는 다루지 않습니다. 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two founders made their first hire. Only one got her time back.
body: Marta makes custom steel brackets. Leo sells scheduling software to physio clinics. Both were working 70-hour weeks. Both hired one person in the same month.
Six months later, Marta still works most evenings. Leo has his Fridays back. The difference wasn't how talented the new person was. It was what the job was.

image.label: Two founders at desks, one buried in paper, one leaving early
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 작은 금속 공방 사무실에서 서류와 메모에 파묻힌 창업자 옆에 조수가 지시를 기다리며 서 있음. 오른쪽은 소프트웨어 회사 책상에서 노트북을 덮고 퇴근하는 창업자, 뒤에서 직원이 혼자 일하고 있음. 실제 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who do you hire first?
body: You run Marta's workshop: four machinists and a steady stream of custom orders. You do the quoting, scheduling, shipping and books yourself.
Late shipments are piling up. Scheduling and shipping take about 25 of your hours each week. You can afford one hire.

options.text: A skilled machinist to raise output
options.feedback: More capacity helps only if the machines are the bottleneck. Here the jam is in planning and shipping, and those still run through you.

options.text: A helper who takes tasks from your list each morning
options.feedback: Cheap and flexible, but every decision still waits for you. You stop doing the work and start assigning and checking it, which saves fewer hours than it seems.

options.text: Someone who owns "every order ships on time," from schedule to truck
options.feedback: This costs more and takes weeks to learn. In return, a whole result leaves your desk, including the decisions inside it.

cards.title: Two hires, two very different weeks.
body: Marta hired a helper. Leo hired someone to own onboarding: getting each new clinic set up and actually using the software in its first two weeks. Founder hours per week:

image.label: Two hires, two very different weeks.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Hire an owner, not extra hands
body: An **owner** is responsible for a result, such as "new clinics are live within two weeks," and decides how to get there. Extra hands do tasks you define.

In a young business, the founder's time is the scarcest resource. A helper still sends every question back to you. An owner takes the questions too. That is why Leo's week shrank and Marta's barely moved.

image.label: Hub diagram vs. a handed-off loop
image.brief: 두 개의 도식 비교. 왼쪽: 창업자가 가운데 있고 모든 화살표("Task", "Question", "Check")가 창업자와 조수 사이를 오감. 오른쪽: 직원이 "Orders ship on time"이라는 원 하나를 혼자 돌리고, 창업자에게는 주간 보고 화살표 하나만 감. 단순한 플랫 인포그래픽.

cards.title: Early hires set the pattern.
body: With five people, one hire is a fifth of the company. How that person works quickly becomes how the company works.

Researchers at Stanford followed about 200 young tech firms in Silicon Valley in the 1990s. Founders' early ideas about whom to hire and how to manage them tended to stick as firms grew. Firms that changed those models later often went through disruption, such as higher staff turnover.
Your first hires aren't just help. They are the template.

cards.title: What to hand over first, and what to keep.
body: Give away work that repeats and that you already understand. If you can describe what "done well" looks like, someone else can own it.
list: **Hand over:** scheduling, dispatch, onboarding, bookkeeping, routine support
**Keep for now:** work you're still figuring out, like how to win your first customers
**Avoid:** hiring for the org chart you hope to have, like a head of marketing with no budget and no team
cards.callout: An owner needs a known result to own. If you can't define it yet, it's still your job.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders often hire a senior specialist too early. If the product still changes every week, a generalist who owns one result, like activation of new accounts, usually helps more.

cards.title: An owner only works if you let go.
body: Ownership needs three things from you: a clear result, the authority to make decisions, and patience while they do it differently than you would. Many founders hire an owner, then check every step. That quietly turns the owner back into extra hands.
Owners also cost more and take longer to find, and a bad early hire is expensive. A short paid trial project before a full commitment can lower the risk.

cards.title: Now it's an app.
body: You run a booking app for dog groomers with 300 paying salons. You spend about 15 hours a week answering support messages, and the same five questions keep coming in. You can afford one hire.

options.text: A senior engineer to ship features faster
options.feedback: Better features might cut some questions over time. But support stays on your plate today, and nobody is tracking which problems matter most.

options.text: A part-time agent who answers from a script and forwards anything unusual to you
options.feedback: Cheap, but the hard questions still land on you. And no one owns fixing why the same five questions keep arriving.

options.text: Someone who owns support: replies within a day, can refund up to a set limit, and reports the top problems weekly
options.feedback: More expensive, but both the answers and the learning leave your desk. The weekly report also tells you what to fix in the product.

cards.title: Hire someone to own a result, not to take orders.
body: Your first hires decide whether the business still runs through you. Give each one a whole outcome, the authority that comes with it, and room to do it their way.
**Try it today:** list the work that took your hours last week. Circle one task that repeats and that you could describe as a result. Write that result as a one-line job.
